title: How to Evaluate a Target-Date Fund for Your Retirement Goals
description: Looking under the hood of 'set it and forget it' funds to find hidden fees and risks.
content:
Target-Date Funds (TDFs) are the default investment for millions of Americans with a 401(k). The premise is simple: pick the year you retire (e.g., 2050), and the fund manages itself. However, not all TDFs are created equal. Some are 'Passive' collections of cheap index funds, while others are 'Active' vehicles stuffed with high-fee underperforming funds. Furthermore, different fund managers have different 'Glide Paths'—some are much riskier near retirement than others. This guide teaches you how to audit your TDF.

Key Takeaways

  • Index vs Active: Always choose a TDF built with Index Funds (Expense Ratio < 0.15%). Avoid those built with Active Funds (ER > 0.60%).
  • To vs Through: Some funds reach their most conservative point at retirement ('To'). Others stay aggressive through retirement. Know which one you own.
  • The Allocation Check: Verify the stock/bond split matches your risk tolerance. A '2050 Fund' from Fidelity might be 90% stocks, while one from Wells Fargo might be 80%.
  • Hidden Fees: Look for 'Acquired Fund Fees' in the prospectus. Ensure there are no layers of double-dipping.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The Department of Labor allows employers to auto-enroll staff into TDFs. While well-intentioned, this creates apathy. Many employees wake up 20 years later to find they paid 1% fees annually, losing 25% of their potential wealth.

Analyzing the 'Glide Path'

The Glide Path determines how fast the fund shifts from Stocks (Growth) to Bonds (Safety).

The 'Through' Strategy (e.g., T. Rowe Price)

These funds assume you will live to 95. They keep a higher percentage of stocks (e.g., 55-60%) even after you retire.
Pros: Higher growth potential needed for long life.
Cons: Higher crash risk. If the market crashes the year you retire, you lose more.

The 'To' Strategy (e.g., BlackRock LifePath)

These funds aim to reach their safest point exactly at age 65. They might hold only 30-40% stocks at retirement.
Pros: Maximum safety at the finish line.
Cons: Inflation risk. Your money might not grow fast enough to last 30 years.

Cost Analysis

Look at the Expense Ratio:

  • Vanguard Target Retirement: 0.08% (Excellent)
  • Fidelity Freedom INDEX: 0.12% (Good)
  • Fidelity Freedom (Active): 0.75% (Avoid)
  • Competitor Active Funds: 1.00%+ (Terrible)

How to Audit Your 401(k)

  1. Log In: Find your current investment holding ticker symbol (e.g., VFFVX).
  2. Google It: Search '[Ticker] Expense Ratio'. If it is above 0.20%, you are paying too much.
  3. Check the Alternative: Does your 401(k) offer separate Index Funds (S&P 500, Bond Market)? If the TDF is expensive, build your own 3-Fund Portfolio using the separate cheap funds.
  4. Check the Date: If you plan to retire early (55), don't buy the 2055 fund (age 65). Buy the 2045 fund. Align the fund date with your financial timeline, not your biological age.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I hold TDFs in a Brokerage Account?

Not recommended. They generate taxable events when they rebalance. Keep them in tax-sheltered accounts (401k/IRA).

Why do TDFs lose money?

They hold stocks and bonds. Both can go down. A TDF is not a savings account; it is an investment portfolio. It will fluctuate.

Can I mix TDFs with other funds?

You shouldn't. A TDF is designed to be a complete meal. Adding an S&P 500 fund on the side tilts your allocation and breaks the glide path logic. Go 100% TDF or 0%.
